name: Colin Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and have answered calls and chats at the contact centre for years. I finished secondary school and handle an ordinary mix of booking and payment problems about as well as the rest of the experienced floor. Evening shifts make my pay higher than usual, though I do not run the team. I use an AI draft occasionally after a colleague has shown me what to check.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Asha, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. She works at a home-care service, and we have about eight months of expenses saved. Plenty of other centres are nearby. I like a call that ends with the correct booking written down; I dislike getting a second call because a tidy note skipped the new date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the evening desk AI Plateau sounds like the draft helper we sometimes use. I would still read back the changed booking date before a customer hangs up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my evening hours are safe in this picture. Eight months saved covers a repair, but it is not a reason to stop checking the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the same evening calls and use the draft only on booking types another agent has tested. In the first year of small change, I’d put part of each evening supplement into the house reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough about work, watchful about mistakes. A neat booking note can still send a family to the wrong door on the wrong day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What booking error sticks with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday a draft kept the original date after a customer moved an appointment. I read the updated line back and caught it before the customer travelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the reserve now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Asha (my partner) and I have the reserve in a separate account. I would keep adding to it before we consider replacing the dining set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take standard booking chats first, so we should compare the weekly paid rota before and after the new system. I would ask for a proper paid vacancy list, not a promise that good agents will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may lose some evening hours, and the premium is what makes this job pay well. Eight months saved lets me choose carefully, but Asha’s care wage does not replace mine under the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d test the new booking checker on fifteen old changed appointments during a paid shift if errors can be logged. In the first year routine bookings move, I’d apply for a posted paid complaints role at a nearby centre only if written wage and hours cover the mortgage and enough of the lost premium; I’d leave only after signing an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota, though I can measure the change. A lost evening shift is a pay cut even when my badge still opens the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which trial result matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count wrong appointment dates and repeat calls, then show the supervisor the list. I need the paid hours beside those figures or the result tells only half the story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare a new role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Asha (my partner) to compare the whole weekly pay with our mortgage and child costs. A day role with a better title can still take money out of our house.

I know **eight months saved** cannot replace my wage forever.
I need a **signed offer** before leaving the evening wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could do the booking and the checking before robots handle physical work. I would ask management for dates and posted paid jobs now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap thinking AI could take my evening headset shifts in 2028. Robots around 2031 do not give me extra phone work; eight months saved is useful, but the mortgage keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d postpone the planned new dining set and keep its money in the reserve. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid stockroom job only if the written wage and hours cover the mortgage; I’d take a paid trial day to see the lifting before treating it as my next trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not without time to look. Eight months of mortgage savings is a bridge to a wage, not a wage of its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Asha about the table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Asha (my partner) the old table works. We can use the new-set money to hold the house if my calls stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the stockroom manager to show me a full paid morning of deliveries. Robots could reach that hands-on work around 2031, so I would not call it permanent safety.

I’d tell colleagues **2028 thinking AI** reaches calls before robots.

I see **eight months saved** as a search bridge.

fieldNote: He understands the **2028 headset risk** and later robot date.

steps.text: Delay the new dining set while the old table still works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn what a stockroom really pays before giving up the phones. I would ask for a posted wage and actual shifts before paying for any course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could get used to physical stock work in five years, but robots around 2034 might later reach it. My evening call wage is worth keeping until a different job proves it can pay the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d ask the stockroom for a paid trial if a real posted opening has mortgage-covering hours and wages. In the first year after 2031, I’d accept that work only on a written offer still meeting those terms; I’d take employer-funded training on paid time if that opening requires it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can test a full shift instead of guessing. A posted wage and a hard morning tell me more than a course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would watch how much lifting and travel the full morning takes. A quiet hour beside a shelf would tell me nothing about the actual day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household cost belongs in the offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Asha (my partner) the offer must cover the mortgage after transport costs. We would keep current call pay until the stockroom manager puts that offer in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives a decade to compare real pay packets and keep the children’s routine steady. I would ask what work the centre will pay people to do each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could keep earning the evening premium for years and save more, though full thinking AI may still take the calls in 2036. Robots around 2039 arrive later for hands-on jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep evening calls and save a fixed part of each premium payment. In the first year after 2036, I’d move to a posted paid service or stock role only if call hours fall and a signed offer covers the mortgage with steady hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant end, calm enough about next year. A decade before AGI in 2036 gives me time to test wages without gambling the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pay figure would you compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read the whole weekly pay before changing jobs. An hourly rate can hide fewer shifts, and we still need the same house payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children in their school unless Asha (my partner) and I had a signed offer and a manageable journey. Several centres nearby give us places to try first.

I know **2036 thinking AI** may still take calls.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could handle the calls that pay our evening rate before I settle into another job. Eight months saved gives us a search window. A posted paid vacancy with hours that cover our mortgage and replace enough of the evening pay, plus early written notice, would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who teaches a new worker the first exception. My father showed me how to check a receipt twice before he let me promise a customer anything.

headlineQuote: My father showed me how to check a receipt twice before he let me promise a customer anything.
portrait: At **43**, Colin is an experienced average-skill agent after secondary school with higher evening pay.
He and Asha support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with eight months saved.
He uses AI **occasionally** after a colleague proves how to check it.
He tests **paid alternatives** before risking the evening wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove evening calls before a new role replaces their mortgage income.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a posted role with hours covering mortgage and lost evening pay would help.
